title: Peter and Paul (29 June)
hookLine: the rock and the tentmaker, remembered on one day

lines: I WITHSTOOD HIM TO THE FACE.
WHO GETS TO SIT AT THE TABLE?
cards: A shared table in Antioch. Peter is eating with gentile believers. Then visitors arrive from James in Jerusalem, and Peter quietly pulls back and keeps himself apart.
Paul doesn't take him aside for a private word. He writes about it later, in the King James Bible: "But when Peter was come to Antioch, I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed."
Two leaders of the young church, disagreeing in public about who gets to sit at the table. And yet the church calendar puts them on the same day: one feast, both names. Today, Peter and Paul.

teach.h: THE ROCK: A FISHERMAN NAMED STONE.
teach.b: They were very different men. Peter was a fisherman from Galilee named Simon.
In John's Gospel, when his brother Andrew brings him to Jesus, Jesus renames him on the spot: "thou shalt be called Cephas, which is by interpretation, A stone."
Later, in Matthew: "thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church." Paul had hunted down Jesus's followers, until a blinding light on the road to Damascus turned him around.
He wrote letters, crossed seas, argued in synagogues and marketplaces, and paid his way with his hands. Acts says of him and his friends, "by their occupation they were tentmakers."
The rock and the tentmaker: one walked Galilee with Jesus, the other met him on a road, after the resurrection. The word pillar comes from Paul himself, in the same letter as the row.
In Jerusalem, "James, Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars," gave him "the right hands of fellowship." A handshake across a real difference: Peter to his own people, Paul to the gentiles.
So the feast doesn't pretend they always agreed.
It holds them side by side, two pillars holding up one roof. Churches read Peter's place differently.
Catholic teaching sees the bishop of Rome as Peter's successor and reads the rock as Peter himself; Orthodox and Protestant Christians understand the rock and Peter's role in other ways.
Tradition says both men died in Rome for their faith. And a letter that carries Peter's name calls Paul "our beloved brother."

how: Catholic, Orthodox and some Anglican and Lutheran churches keep Peter and Paul together on one feast day, reading of Peter's confession and of Paul's ministry.

games.q: you're Paul in Antioch. Peter, a leader you respect, has pulled back from eating with gentile believers. what do you do?
o: withstand him to his face, in front of everyone.
games.why: Paul confronts him publicly. yet in the same letter he tells of the right hands of fellowship, and the church remembers both on one day.

practice: Bring to mind two people you love who are nothing alike, one loud and one quiet, maybe two who'd argue if you put them in a room. Hold each in turn, and what they give you that nobody else does.
If you pray, thank God for each by name; if you don't, be grateful for them one at a time, and notice how both hold up something in your life.
